Prevention: Deep planting: planting tuber seed at a depth of 5-10 cm prevents female moths from ovipositing in seed tubers and keeps larvae from migrating to tubers from infested sprouts above ground
High hilling of growing plants protects the developing tubers from ovipositing females and reduces the possibility of larvae reaching the bulking tubers
Frequent irrigation prevents cracks from forming in the soil, which would allow female moths to reach potato tubers for laying eggs and provide shelter for adult moths
During harvest, select healthy tubers, defoliate when the crop is mature and remove harvest residues from the field
Store harvested tubers immediately or cover; do not leave exposed tubers overnight when females lay eggs
Crop rotation; the potato tuber moth attacks potato tubers only
Monitoring: Larvae feed exclusively on potato tubers in the field and in store.
At early stages, the symptoms are not visible externally.
Cut open the tuber and look for larval damage, including the presence of frass in dark coloured galleries
Circular exit holes (around 2-3 mm in diameter) on the surface of the potato tuber
If the tubers have been infected for a long time, the tubers might be rotten
Brown adult moths may be observed in the field at dusk, when they fly around or gather in the border of the crop, amongst weeds
Set pheromone traps (16/ha) and check weekly to detect the level of adults in the field
Damage looks similar to other species of potato tuber moth
Take action when you detect symptoms, or presence of larvae and moths
Direct Control: In the field, use sex pheromone traps or light traps (16/ha from planting to harvest)
Use bioinsecticides (e.g. dusting seed tubers with a powder preparation of the virus
When infestation is severe, clean carefully (periodic elimination of damaged tubers) and use diffused lighting (results in greening of the tubers which is unfavourable for the moth)
Use one pheromone trap to disrupt mating during storage
